solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Balls inverted after bottom of pants turned in — nasty

indicators.note: the bottom of a word written across is its end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of pants

indicators.note: something turned faces the other way, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: taken as written, then flipped to NI

indicators.note: turned upside down, which in a written word means read back to front

parts.note: Ed Balls, the Labour politician, supplies his first name, flipped to DE

explanation.surface: A crude jibe: something upside down and turned in at the seat of the trousers, and very nasty with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls' is not a body part here but Ed Balls, the former Labour shadow chancellor, whose first name is flipped; 'in' is a word to be turned, not a position.
explanation.definitionFit: A snide remark is sneering and mean-spirited, so the word works as an adjective for spiteful unpleasantness.

clue.text: About to turn against Labour? That won't be a problem

indicators.note: turning round makes the letters face the other way and read backwards

parts.note: on means about, as in a book on birds
sweat is hard toil, labour

explanation.surface: A politician asks whether to turn against the Labour party, and is told it will be no trouble at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Labour' with its capital looks like the political party, but it is plain hard work; 'against' simply sets the two parts side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase is an idiom used to reassure someone that a task is easy and causes no difficulty.

clue.text: (& 5dn.) How to stress something Boris & co wanted us to do about Partygate

definitions.meaning: first meaning: literally underline a written word to emphasise it

definitions.text: Boris & co wanted us to do about Partygate
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the idiom for declaring a matter closed and moving on

explanation.walkthrough: Partygate was the scandal over lockdown parties held in Downing Street under Boris Johnson, whose government repeatedly urged the public to move on from it.
explanation.definitionFit: Underlining is the literal way to add emphasis in writing, and the same phrase is an idiom for closing a matter and forgetting about it.

clue.text: Promotion of lousy independent leaders secured by local financial centre

indicators.note: something secured by another is held fast within it, so one piece sits inside

parts.note: a local is the pub nearest your home

indicators.note: leaders go in front, so each word gives up only its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letters of lousy and independent
the City is London's financial district

explanation.surface: A dismal independent candidate gets a promotional push from the business district's local bigwigs.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials sit between the two other parts; 'local' is British slang for one's regular pub, and the City means the Square Mile of London finance.
explanation.definitionFit: Publicity is the attention a product or person gets from advertising, a close synonym of promotion.

clue.text: see 3dn.
Robert Maxwell type in the limelight? "One little reptile!"

parts.note: lit up by the spotlight
the Roman numeral for one
a gator is a shortened alligator

explanation.surface: A press baron basks in publicity while someone mutters that he is nothing but a small reptile.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Maxwell, the fraudulent newspaper tycoon, was famous for suing Private Eye repeatedly; 'little' shortens alligator rather than meaning a young one.
explanation.definitionFit: Maxwell constantly took critics to court, so a person who habitually files lawsuits is an example of his type.

clue.text: Wow — a LibDem leader that's endangered in the main!

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for 'something that is endangered at sea'

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise
taken as written

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the first letter of LibDem

explanation.surface: Surprise at a Liberal Democrat leader who is endangered for the most part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the main' reads as 'mostly', but the main is the old poetic word for the open sea; cor is a British working-class 'wow'.
explanation.definitionFit: Coral reefs are threatened by warming and acidifying oceans, so coral is a living thing at risk under the sea.

clue.text: Emblem of a nation's awful shit time, dogged by the French

indicators.note: to be dogged is to be followed closely, so the next piece comes directly after
something awful is in a bad state, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
T is the abbreviation for time
le is the French for the

explanation.surface: A country living through a dreadful period, hounded all the while by the French.
explanation.walkthrough: The rude word is rearranged, followed by the abbreviation for time and the French definite article.
explanation.definitionFit: The prickly purple flower is the national symbol of Scotland, so it is the floral emblem of a nation.

clue.text: (&24dn.) Music genre expert finally getting pitch

parts.note: a pro is a professional, an expert

indicators.note: finally points to the end of a word, so its last letter alone is kept

parts.note: the last letter of getting
a ship pitches when it sways fore and aft in a swell, and a four-letter word for that swaying is wanted

explanation.surface: A music critic finally lands the right tone or note for a genre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' looks musical in this surface, but it is the verb for tossing to and fro, as a boat does on waves.
explanation.definitionFit: Progressive rock is the 1970s style of long, complex songs, and a genre is a category of music.

clue.text: Branded second vehicle, loud colour

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
a car is a vehicle
red is the classic loud, bright colour

explanation.surface: A second car with brash branding, painted in a garish colour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Branded' suggests a logo on the vehicle, but it is the definition, meaning marked by burning.
explanation.definitionFit: Branding with a hot iron leaves a permanent mark on the skin, so to be branded is to be marked for life.

clue.text: Putin's about to imprison dissenter, finally — idiot!

indicators.note: about means all around and in disorder, so the letters are scattered and rearranged

parts.note: the Russian leader's surname, taken as written

indicators.note: finally points to the end of a word, so only its last letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of dissenter

explanation.surface: Putin is on the point of jailing a dissident, and the writer calls him a fool.
explanation.walkthrough: The Russian leader's name is jumbled with one letter taken inside it; 'to imprison' just says that letter goes into the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: Turnip is British slang for a dim-witted person, a vegetable used as an insult for stupidity.

clue.text: Write article on no good state of Malaysia

parts.note: to pen is to write
a is the indefinite article
NG is the abbreviation for no good

explanation.surface: An instruction to write a piece about how badly things are going in a Malaysian state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Article' looks like a newspaper piece to be written, but it is the grammatical article.
explanation.definitionFit: Penang is an island state on the north-west coast of peninsular Malaysia, home to George Town.

clue.text: To control urge, let cycling absorb one

indicators.note: cycling sends things round and round, so the letters end up in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a means one

explanation.surface: Advice on curbing an impulse: let taking up cycling soak it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycling' reads as a hobby that burns off urges; 'absorb' just tells you to take the extra letter into the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: To regulate is to govern or keep in check by rules, a close synonym of controlling.

clue.text: US's last missile? That's harsh

indicators.note: the last of a word is its end, so only the closing letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter of US
Trident is a submarine-launched nuclear missile

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether America's final weapon is a missile, and judges that a severe step.
explanation.walkthrough: Trident is the nuclear missile system used by both the US and the UK.
explanation.definitionFit: A strident voice or tone is loud and grating, one sense of harsh.

clue.text: Issue with new city limits — crisis!

parts.note: to issue is to come out, emerge
N is the abbreviation for new

indicators.note: limits are the edges of something, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters of city

explanation.surface: A problem arises with the new boundaries of a city, and it is a crisis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Issue' looks like a noun meaning a problem, but it is the verb for coming out.
explanation.definitionFit: An emergency is a sudden dangerous situation needing urgent action, which is what a crisis is.

clue.text: Knock over Grant: it might make you feel better

definitions.text: it might make you feel better

indicators.note: knocked over means turned upside down, so the letters read back to front

parts.note: to bat is to hit or knock
to let is to allow or grant

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to floor a man called Grant, on the grounds that it would be therapeutic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' with a capital looks like a person to be knocked over; it is the verb meaning allow.
explanation.definitionFit: A tablet is a pill of medicine, taken to relieve symptoms and help the patient recover.

clue.text: Gore's against Conservative crowd: not good for circulation

parts.note: gore is spilt blood
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
a lot is a group or crowd

explanation.surface: Al Gore opposes the Tory mob, a stance unhelpful to a newspaper's sales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gore' suggests Al Gore and 'circulation' newspaper sales; both are medical here, gore being blood and circulation the flow round the body.
explanation.definitionFit: A clump of thickened blood can block a vessel, obstructing the flow of blood through the body.

clue.text: See about stuffing a revolutionary, to follow dessert?

definitions.note: stands for 'something to follow dessert', a noun

indicators.note: stuffing goes inside something, so one piece is packed into another

parts.note: Che Guevara, the Argentine revolutionary

indicators.note: brought about means turned round, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: taken as written, then turned to EES

explanation.surface: A dinner plan: look into filling a Marxist guerrilla, perhaps after pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: The reversed word goes between the second and third letters of the revolutionary's name.
explanation.definitionFit: In a British formal meal a cheese course is often served after the sweet course, so it follows dessert.

clue.text: What those in low-cut dresses might do to relax

definitions.text: What those in low-cut dresses might do
definitions.meaning: first meaning: literally spill out or dangle from a revealing neckline
second meaning: the informal verb for spending idle time somewhere

explanation.surface: Women in plunging necklines wonder how to unwind.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a saucy literal reading of the phrasal verb; the second is its everyday informal sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To spend time idly or casually with friends is the informal phrasal verb's everyday sense of unwinding.

clue.text: Overcome knight said to assume bonking position

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the piece is spelt by its sound rather than its usual form

parts.note: a knight is addressed as Sir
to mount is to climb on top, as in sex

explanation.surface: A knight, reportedly overwhelmed, is urged into a sexual position.
explanation.walkthrough: Bonking is British slang for having sex; in a non-rhotic British accent SIR and SUR sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: To surmount an obstacle is to get over it, the same as overcoming it.

clue.text: Rolling Stones taking temperature, as protection from the Texas sun?

indicators.note: rolling things tumble over, so the letters land in a different order

parts.note: taken as written
T is the abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: The Rolling Stones check the thermometer while touring Texas, needing shade from the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: The band's name splits: 'Rolling' is the signal and 'Stones' the letters, with the temperature abbreviation added to them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stetson is the wide-brimmed cowboy hat, worn in Texas to shade the head from strong sunshine.

clue.text: Sort to fiddle around in sweet Fanny Adams's orifice

indicators.note: one thing placed around another encloses it, so the outer piece wraps the inner

parts.note: sweet Fanny Adams is British slang for nothing at all

indicators.note: to fiddle with something is to mess it about, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged

explanation.surface: A crude invitation to poke about in some woman's bodily opening.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweet Fanny Adams (sweet FA) is British slang for nothing, so NIL, which wraps the jumbled letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A nostril is one of the two openings of the nose, so it is a bodily orifice.

clue.text: One has drunk gin with true artifice

indicators.note: someone drunk staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone who has knocked back gin is being truly crafty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has drunk gin' reads as drinking, but 'drunk' is the signal to jumble the letters of one, gin and true together.
explanation.definitionFit: Intrigue is secret scheming and plotting, which is cunning trickery in the sense of artifice.

clue.text: Something from the past brought up by some imbecile reactionary

indicators.note: in a down clue, bringing something up means reading it from bottom to top
some means only part of, so the letters lie inside the following words

parts.note: the letters spanning the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: An old grievance is dredged up by a foolish reactionary.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the join of the two words and are read upwards in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A relic is an object or custom surviving from an earlier age, a thing left over from history.

clue.text: Plant Cyclops had twisted round in hives?

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: hives is an itchy skin rash

indicators.note: to twist something round is to turn it about so it faces the other way

parts.note: Cyclops is the setter, so I; had contracts to 'd

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to a plant he wound round some beehives.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's name stands for 'I', so 'Cyclops had' gives I'D; 'hives' is the skin complaint, not beehives.
explanation.definitionFit: The radish is a plant grown for its crisp, peppery red root, eaten raw in salads.

clue.text: see 9dn.
Ballot measurement that can be irritating

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for 'something that can be irritating'

parts.note: a poll is a vote, a ballot
an en is a printer's unit of measurement

explanation.surface: A complaint that counting votes is a tiresome business.
explanation.walkthrough: The en is a printer's measure of width, half an em; 'irritating' points to the nose and eyes, not a vote count.
explanation.definitionFit: Pollen grains from plants trigger hay fever, inflaming the nose and eyes of allergic people.

clue.text: Non-religious clause removed by Republican

indicators.note: re-moved means moved again, so the letters are shifted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A Republican lawmaker strikes a church-and-state clause from a bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Removed' reads as deleted, but it signals moving the letters again, a less common anagram indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: Secular describes worldly matters with no connection to religion or the church.

clue.text: Unpleasant climax with sweaty bum

parts.note: sweaty skin is sticky
your end is your backside

explanation.surface: A smutty picture of a disappointing orgasm and a damp backside.
explanation.walkthrough: Bum is British slang for bottom, and the 'end' is the rear end.
explanation.definitionFit: Coming to a sticky end is a British idiom for a nasty death or bad outcome, an unpleasant conclusion.

clue.text: Hackneyed introduction to Sun story

indicators.note: an introduction comes at the start, so only the opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of Sun
a tale is a story

explanation.surface: A worn-out opening paragraph to a tabloid news story.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper, which makes 'story' look journalistic.
explanation.definitionFit: Hackneyed means overused and unoriginal, just as stale ideas have lost their freshness.
